name: Nora Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43, have a two-year technical diploma and lead a crew that repairs electricity lines while the power is still on. The insulated gloves and bucket are ordinary equipment to me, but I never let an apprentice forget the voltage test. I enjoy teaching at the company yard; concentrating through a long live-line shift is what wears me down.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are things at home, and do you use AI tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works in hospital records, and we have two school-age children, a mortgage and about four months of expenses saved. My pay is typical for this work, and a few other line crews are within commuting distance. I use AI now and then to draft a training note, but I check every safety step against the approved manual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that a quicker work order is useful, but it does not test a live wire. Our insulated tools and the person checking them still make the job safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My lead lineworker post should hold, and the mortgage has four months of expenses behind it. My partner's hospital records work includes routine forms, though, so even a small software saving could press on those hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the live-line rota and teach the apprentices how to repeat a voltage test before lifting anything. Each month I'll use the AI writing tool I already know for the training handout, then compare its instructions with the approved manual before giving it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my partner's hours, though I feel steady on the line crew. We could handle a short setback, not a long one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where has the writing tool got a safety step wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week the tool put the rubber glove check after the lift in a draft handout. I moved it back before the lift and showed the apprentices the approved sequence. The AI handout put the rubber glove check after the lift; my apprentices need that check before it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you cut spending based on a worry alone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my partner for the actual hospital rota before changing our spending. If the hours stay steady, we keep the current mortgage payment and the four-month reserve.

say: **Live-wire tests** still need a trained crew, even if software speeds up routine work orders.
**Training handouts** must match the approved safety sequence, whatever writes the draft.
think: My **lineworker role** looks secure in the mild picture.
My partner's **records hours** may face pressure from small changes in routine screen work.
do: **Keep** the live-line rota and teach apprentices the approved voltage-test sequence.
**Check** any AI-drafted handout against the approved manual before use.
feel: **Anxious** about records hours, though confident in my own crew.
S0.quote: The AI handout put the rubber glove check after the lift; my apprentices need that check before it.
fieldNote: She uses an **occasional AI draft** but anchors training in the approved safety manual.
Her **four-month cushion** eases a short setback while partner records hours remain a concern.

steps.text: Keep live-line rota and teach approved voltage-test sequence

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say buying, booking and paperwork may move quickly to software, while field robots come more slowly. On live lines, I want proof of how any new plan handles the isolation points before we send a bucket up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own hands-on work still needs a crew, but my partner's records position could lose hours as the hospital automates forms. Four months of savings gives us time, yet the mortgage depends on two regular pay packets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the supervisor to let me compare three generated switching plans with the paper diagrams and field markings. If the checks pass, I'll take the company's paid tool training and show apprentices how to challenge a bad plan; at home we'll track my partner's hours monthly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the household income, though I can manage the changes on my crew. The screen can be wrong in a way that looks tidy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens when diagram and pole disagree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stop the bucket below the line and ask control to confirm the switch position. A disagreement between the diagram and the pole is a reason to pause, not a puzzle for an apprentice to solve alone. A tidy switching plan can still send my apprentice's bucket toward the wrong live wire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut if the records hours fall?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my partner loses a shift, we'd first trim the weekend food budget and leave the emergency reserve for mortgage payments. I would wait for an actual rota change before claiming that this happened.

say: **Generated switching plans** need a field check before live-line crews work.
**Desk paperwork** will change faster than bucket work in this slower disruption.
think: My partner's **records hours** could shrink even while my lineworker job remains.
Four months of **savings** buys time but cannot cover a long drop in household pay.
do: **Compare** three generated switching plans with diagrams and field markings.
**Take** company-paid tool training if those checks pass.
feel: **Anxious** about the household wage and confident enough to test new plans.
S1.quote: A tidy switching plan can still send my apprentice's bucket toward the wrong live wire.
fieldNote: She describes a **three-plan test** before accepting training, consistent with proven change.
The possible loss of **partner hours** raises her mood beyond mere unease about surrounding change.

steps.text: Compare three generated switching plans with field markings
Take company-paid planner training if three checks pass

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues thinking AI by 2028 could handle hospital records and electricity dispatch before robots work live lines around 2031. Our company needs to say which crew jobs and safety roles it intends to keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might keep my line wage until the robots arrive, but my partner's records hours could fall earlier. If we lost that income, four months of savings would run out while the mortgage kept coming. Four months of savings cannot carry our mortgage through a long loss of hospital records pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll ask both employers for staffing plans and ask my company about paid live-line robot testing posts. We'll stop the proposed new car deposit and put a fixed amount from each future pay packet into emergency savings; if a paid testing post opens, I'll apply while I still have my crew wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with some control because I can test new equipment and there are a few nearby line crews. I would be much more frightened by an actual notice than by this imagined date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about the car?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the children a new car is off for now and that school costs remain in the plan. I would not call their other parent's hospital job lost without a staffing notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes a testing position real enough to apply for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would apply only if the testing post has a wage and supervised live-line work. Reading a course brochure will not replace our partner income or cover the mortgage.

say: **2028 thinking AI** could reach records and dispatch before live-line robots arrive around 2031.
The company should publish **crew and safety roles** with real pay attached.
think: My partner's **records income** might shrink before my physical linework does.
Four months of **savings** would not cover a long gap in one household wage.
do: **Ask** both employers for staffing plans and any paid robot testing openings.
**Cancel** the proposed car deposit and cut that planned purchase.
**Save** a fixed amount from future wages while both jobs still pay.
feel: **Anxious** about possible household pay loss, with some options still open.
S2.quote: Four months of savings cannot carry our mortgage through a long loss of hospital records pay.
fieldNote: She treats partner work as the **earlier exposure** and her field work as later robot exposure.
She has **no job notice** and avoids claiming a certain loss or panic.
Her proposed savings come from **future wages**, while the car purchase is cancelled.

steps.text: Ask both employers for staffing plans and paid testing openings
Cancel proposed car deposit and planned purchase
Save fixed amount from future wages while both jobs pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years allows a measured live-line robot trial before the 2034 field date. The 2031 thinking system might change plans first, so any robot still needs a named person who can stop it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could qualify to inspect robot work if a paid opening exists. The risk is spending years teaching new checks while our line shifts quietly thin out and my partner's records job changes too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask for a supervised company trial with control of the stop switch, and take the paid operator course if it is offered after the trial. At home we'll make a small extra mortgage payment from regular wages each month, but stop that overpayment if records hours fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about both pay packets, but the extra time lets me test rather than guess. I can accept a machine that passes hard checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you make the robot demonstrate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have it approach a live-line training rig and make it stop for a planted fault. A live-line robot that cannot stop for a planted fault has no place near the public network.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would the extra mortgage money come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The overpayment comes from the children's old sports travel budget now that practices are nearer home. It is new money from each wage, not the four months we already saved.

say: **Supervised trials** need a clear human stop before live-line robots arrive around 2034.
**2031 planning AI** changes the desk first; field checks still decide whether a robot is safe.
think: A paid **inspection opening** might suit me, but none has been promised.
Our two **income streams** remain exposed as records work and line shifts change.
do: **Control** a trial stop switch on a supervised live-line training rig.
**Take** a paid operator course if offered after a successful trial.
**Overpay** the mortgage from current wages while records hours hold.
feel: **Anxious** about hours, but willing to test proven field equipment.
S3.quote: A live-line robot that cannot stop for a planted fault has no place near the public network.
fieldNote: Her planned trial includes **hands-on control**, so the new-tool learning is concrete.
She conditions the course on a **paid offer** and a successful supervised trial.
Mortgage overpayments are **new payments** from wages and pause if records hours fall.

steps.text: Control stop switch on supervised live-line robot trial if offered
Take paid robot operator course if offered after successful trial
Overpay mortgage from wages while partner records hours hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives us time to train apprentices in both line safety and robot oversight. Thinking AI by 2036 would handle more planning, while capable live-line robots around 2039 would be the real test for the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 56 I might choose a paid safety instructor role if one exists. I would still need a regular wage; the mortgage and two children do not disappear because the technology date is later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep my technical diploma skills current through the company safety refreshers and ask each year which paid instructor vacancies exist. We'll keep the four-month reserve intact and review the mortgage balance each year before making any career move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not losing sleep over a decade-long path. I can see room for a careful transition if the employer actually funds it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would apprentices need to learn alongside robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd let an apprentice see a robot alongside the insulated tools, then ask them to explain the stop rule back to me. They should know why a device is safe, not simply that it has a company sticker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a safety instructor post viable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The instructor post needs a full roster, field practice and pay close to my line wage. I would not leave my live-line bucket for a handful of guest lessons.

say: **Apprentices** need line tests and robot stop rules before field machines arrive around 2039.
**2036 planning AI** gives the company time to develop paid field safety roles.
think: A paid **instructor role** might fit at 56 if a proper vacancy exists.
Our **mortgage** still needs a regular wage, even with ten years to prepare.
do: **Keep** technical line safety skills current through company refreshers.
**Check** paid instructor vacancies each year for roster, field practice and wages.
feel: **Uneasy** about later roles, with time to plan if posts are funded.
S4.quote: I would not leave my live-line bucket for a handful of guest lessons.
fieldNote: She makes a later move **conditional** on a real instructor vacancy with comparable wages.
Her focus stays on **paid safety practice** and an apprentice's ability to explain the stop rule.

steps.text: Keep line safety skills current through company refreshers
Check paid instructor vacancies annually for full roster and wages

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my partner's records job could change before live-line robots arrive around 2031. Published staffing plans for both workplaces and a paid robot testing post, if one opens, would help us plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who is allowed to stop a robot on a live wire. A stop switch belongs within reach of a trained lineworker, not buried in a manager's dashboard. That rule would tell me whether the company really understands the job. A stop switch for a live-line robot belongs within reach of a trained lineworker, not buried in a manager's dashboard.

headlineQuote: A stop switch for a live-line robot belongs within reach of a trained lineworker, not buried in a manager's dashboard.
portrait: **Nora**, 43, leads live-line repairs and teaches apprentices after earning a two-year technical diploma.
She uses **AI occasionally** for notes but checks every safety step against the approved manual.
Her **four-month reserve** and typical pay support a mortgage, while partner hospital records hours may face earlier change.
She would test **robot stop controls** herself and consider a paid instructor role only with a full roster.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could affect partner records pay before live-line robots arrive around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: Published **staffing plans** and a paid robot testing vacancy, if available, would help the household decide.
